newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Two Nigerian lawyers vow to defend detained Abiola.
newsitem.headline: Two Nigerian lawyers vow to defend detained Abiola.

text.p: Two radical Nigerian opposition lawyers recently released from detention offered on Wednesday free legal services to detained presidential claimant Moshood Abiola and vowed to ensure he regained his freedom.

Gani Fawehinmi and Femi Falana told a news conference in Lagos that they intended to challenge the authorities to proceed with the stalled treason trial of Abiola, who has been held since 1994 when he proclaimed himself president in defiance of the army.
"On our own part, our two chambers are prepared to put all our professional and legal resources at the disposal of Chief M.K.O. Abiola free of charge," Fawehinmi said.
Two other top lawyers are already fighting over who should represent Abiola in his treason trial.
Fawehinmi and Falana said they would appeal to those two lawyers to ... "consider the interest of Abiola, million of voters and the future of Nigeria and withdraw from the case."

The two lawyers are implacable foes of the military government and were themselves freed from nearly a year in detention last November when a Commonwealth mission visited Nigeria over human rights and restoration of democracy.

Abiola, a multi-millionaire businessman believed to have won an annulled 1993 presidential election, has not been seen in public since August 1994 when he last appeared in court on charges of treason.
The case became stalled after the judge withdrew because Abiola said he could not get fair hearing from him. Since then there have also been a series of other court suits.
The annulment of the 1993 poll plunged Africa's most populous nation into political crisis.

Military ruler General Sani Abacha, who seized power in the chaos that followed the annulment, is implementing a transition plan he says will see him hand power to a democratically-elected president in October 1998.
Critics of the Abacha government have dismissed the transition programme, saying it was taking too long and that the he intends to use it to retain power.
